newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka rebels seek India leader's support.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka rebels seek India leader's support.

text.p: Sri Lanka's Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels said on Thursday they hoped that India's new prime minister would support the self-determination rights of Tamils in the island's north and east.

"Tamils in the northeast of Sri Lanka are really encouraged you have assumed duties as Indian prime minister. We hope you will support the self-determination rights of the Tamils and also expect that you will speak against the Sri Lankan army's occupation of Tamil land," said the Voice of Tigers radio.

The clandestine radio, monitored in Vavuniya, 220 km (138 miles) north of Colombo, quoted an LTTE letter to Inder Kumar Gujral as saying Tamils in Sri Lanka's northeast wanted to maintain a strategic and historical relationship with India.

"We are not only related to Tamils in (India's southern state of) Tamil Nadu, but also share the vast cultural values. We hope our relationship and the contacts with the people of India will continue in the coming years," the radio quoted the letter as saying.
The LTTE have been fighting for more than 13 years for a separate homeland for minority Tamils in Sri Lanka's north and east.
Gujral, during a visit to Sri Lanka in January as foreign minister, had said India would do what it could to end the war.
"India is ready to provide Sri Lanka any help she could give," Gujral said then. But he added that New Delhi supported a peaceful settlement of the conflict.
"We are committed to a policy of good neighbourliness and non-intereference in Sri Lanka's affairs," Gujral said.
India sent troops to Sri Lanka under a 1987 peace accord to end the civil war. The Indian troops were withdrawn in 1990 after an inconclusive campaign.

"The Indian government's position on the Sri Lankan ethnic problem as well as on the LTTE has been made abundantly clear. India shuns the LTTE and has endorsed the Sri Lanka government's current approach to solving the ethnic problem," a Sri Lanka Foreign Ministry spokesman told Reuters on Wednesday.
"We are confident that there would be no change in India's percpetion and understanding of our problems," he said.
Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Lakshman Kadirgamar left on Thursday for a two-day goodwill visit to India, where he will meet Gujral and other Indian officials.
